tier_reason: The README table gives this implementation's own 0.0932 cpb (5.964 cycles per 64-byte output) on an unnamed AMD EPYC. The baseline rows (ChaCha8/ChaCha20 AVX-512, VAES, PCG32/XorShift128+, mt19937) are approximate '~' ranges with no sign they were measured in the same run. The repo holds only the header, README, LICENSE and a chart: no benchmark harness, compiler or flags. First-party, no methodology, so C, with the >50x gap versus mt19937 also forcing the cap.

corrections.caveats: Baseline rows are approximate ranges, not shown as measured in the same run. The repo has no benchmark source (only AVX512-VAES2-PRNG.h, README.md, LICENSE and throughput_chart.png, whose bars omit mt19937), and no CPU model, compiler or flags are given. The 43-64x figure versus mt19937 rests on an unmeasured 4-6 cpb range that looks pessimistic for a modern compiled mt19937. By the page's own table, ChaCha8 with AVX-512 (~0.08-0.18 cpb, 'equivalent to the fastest range') matches or beats it, so the clear win is only over scalar non-cryptographic PRNGs. The README mentions 6.04 cycles per output in its prose and 5.964 in the table. Statistical testing is thin: home-grown 'SmallCrush/PractRand equivalent' statistics, plus a claimed TestU01 SmallCrush pass and 0.962 GiB of PractRand. It is not a vetted CSPRNG (the author invites cryptanalysis), needs AVX-512 + VAES + GFNI, and the repo was created on 2026-09-15 with 0 stars. Keep as a flagged proof-of-concept.

notes: README numbers match the record. All 11 commits are dated 2026-09-15, so last_commit and active status are right. Nothing to measure the baseline ranges against.

corrections.caveats: First-party README. The ns/KiB table gives no compiler, flags, hardware or benchmark code. Its links (xoshiro256** to .NET System.Random docs, xoroshiro128++ to Java docs) and SFMT19937 coming out slower than MT19937 suggest managed, non-SIMD implementations of the baselines. So the 9.3x versus MT19937 does not describe std::mt19937 or a SIMD SFMT. The System.Random table names .NET 8 preview on an i7-12700F, but its BenchmarkDotNet harness is not published. CC0 grants no patent rights (no patent grant). Not cryptographically secure: the README says the state was recovered from three outputs with Z3. Needs SSE4/PCLMUL/FMA in C. The latest commit (2023-05-25) is more than 3 years old.

notes: Every number in the record matches the README. The table also has Lehmer128, Shishua and xorshift rows, all slower than Culumi. Four commits, all on 2023-05-25; 4 stars.

tier_reason: benchmark.out shows DualMix128 0.401 ns/call against a correct xoroshiro128++ (0.829 ns) and wyrand (0.401 ns), from the public benchmark.c built with gcc 11.4.0 -O3 -march=native. No CPU model is stated anywhere, so it falls short of A and stays first-party C.

corrections.caveats: First-party. benchmark.c and its output give the gcc version and flags but no CPU model. The xoroshiro128++ in benchmark.c is the standard algorithm. DualMix128 and wyrand both land on exactly 0.401 ns/call with a volatile store per call, which suggests a loop or store floor, so the 2.07x over xoroshiro128++ mainly reflects xoroshiro's longer dependency chain. The update is nonlinear with no proven period; the README strikes through its 'possibly injective' claim, and the repo says it was replaced by LoopMix128 for proven injectivity and a guaranteed 2^128 period. The LoopMix128 URL (danielcota/LoopMix128) now serves the biski64 repository, and biski64 is already catalogued. DualMix128 is a different algorithm, not a copy. Statistical claims (README): PractRand from 256MB to 8TB (32TB in the feature list) with zero anomalies, and BigCrush passed. Speed ties wyrand.

notes: Numbers and flags match benchmark.out and the README. last_commit 2025-05-10 ('Update README.md') confirmed, so stale is right. Kept rather than filed as a duplicate, because the algorithm differs from biski64.
